message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/<area>-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999 via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session) ; `alloc_id()` for element ids (from `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case, from the catalog), snapshots the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (which calls every module's `check(pr)`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step labelled by the command's catalog label (`always_step` hooks force a step even when nothing changed).
- `src/commands/mod.rs` (dispatch: each module's `dispatch(s, cid, p)` is tried in turn), `src/commands/basic.rs` (new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid; `open_path`, `write_atomic`), `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers producing the original's texts: `` `x` in mm is required``, ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9), `src/model.rs` (levels by elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` with the original's errors, `find` by id/GUID, `normalize_guid`), `src/check.rs` (core rules: level/grid; your rules go in your module's `check`).
- Done by others (reuse, don't redo): `src/rvt/` (Revit import; `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a planar-faces tracer and `src/rvt/rooms.rs` a room-enclosure test), `src/cloud/` (point clouds), `src/deflate.rs` (zlib/deflate byte-identical to the original's flate2: `zlib_compress` fast, `zlib_compress_level`), `src/inflate.rs`, `src/util.rs` (base64, fnv1a64), `src/media/` (pictures, `material`, `favorite`, `library`, `paint`), `src/styles/` (line/fill patterns, line styles, region/text/dimension types, line weights, object styles, units, room_area, language, standard, phase, phase_filter, option, parameter, voltage, distribution_system, wire_type, reinforcement_preset; `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` give new/copied elements their phase/option params; `styles::parameters::key_of` for project parameter keys), `src/mcp/`.
- Being written in parallel by others (don't implement these; if you need one, write a minimal private stand-in inside your area and note it): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors, ceilings, shafts, roofs, dormers, rooms, room separators, stairs, ramps, railings, masses and by-face, sketch/edit_boundary/edit_shape/add_point/add_split_line/reset_shape/falls, flip, show_mass; `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`), STRUCTURE (column, structural_column, footing, beam, strip_footing, pipe, duct, conduit, cable_tray, wire, down_conductor, ground_conductor, cabling, rebar, reinforce, type, family, symbol_set, component, the sizing calculators; `src/structure/`), VIEWS (sections, elevations, sheets, place, crop, duplicate_view, scale, detail, visual_style, graphics, filter, template, section_box, perspective, graphic_display_options, camera, work_plane, text, dimension*, tag, spot, spot_slope, detail_line and its join/explode/vertex/convert_spline/offset/trim_extend, filled_region, groups, linework, make_fill_pattern; `src/views/`), EDIT (modify, move, copy, rotate, mirror, corner, split, fillet, align, match_properties, delete, insert, link, reload, purge, delete_type, rename_type, autosave, recover; `src/edit/`), READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, measure, select_by_id, ids_of, filter_selection, and the project-file loader `src/load.rs`; `src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`), IFC-EXPORT (`src/ifc/export*`), IFC-IMPORT (`src/ifc/import*`). Rendering (render, PNG/SVG/PDF/GLB), CAD/DXF, the sample house and the highrise come later.

## How to test
`MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels exactly. Useful trick: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`) and run both programs on that file — the loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params` text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases, every error and the order of checks). Learn element formats from the original's saved files.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't; edits outside your area; what other areas must provide or call.

## YOUR AREA: ARCH (`src/arch/`, `src/geom/`)
Commands: `wall`, `door`, `window`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `shaft`, `roof` (boundary from walls, overhang, slopes, gables, courtyards, extrusion, openings, join), `dormer`, `room`, `room_separator`, `stair`, `ramp`, `railing`, `mass`, `mass_floors`, `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face`, `roof_by_face`, `update_by_face`, `show_mass`, `sketch`, `edit_boundary`, `edit_shape`, `add_point`, `add_split_line`, `reset_shape`, `falls`, `flip`. Their replies, errors, saved JSON and the model rules for these categories (in your `check`: e.g. doors/windows must fit their wall and not overlap, outlines must be simple with the original's wording naming the edges, wall heights, stair/ramp limits…; observe what `move`/`modify` refusals say, as those rules run after every command). Build `src/geom/` as the shared 2D geometry library: polygons (area, orientation, point-in-polygon, simplicity with edge reports), the planar graph of wall centre lines and room separators with room enclosure (which walls bound a room at the level's computation height, room_bounding, islands, redundant rooms in the same space), the outline of a level's walls (floor/roof defaults, courtyards), wall faces and offsets (roof overhang past faces, ceiling to wall faces), sketch solving (`sketch`'s loops, problems and limits). Doors/windows with `family`: a family type's `Width`/`Height`/`Sill Height` come from the project's `families` section (its parameters may hold formulas — the STRUCTURE agent writes the formula engine; read plain values and note formulas). Mark numbering (`P1`→`P2`, `J-09`→`J-10`). Wall `location` lines, `attach_top`/`attach_base`, `top_level`/`top_offset`/`height`, `arc`. Use the test assets' expected IFC files to see which scenarios matter (e.g. `/workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/*.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_model_geometry/*.ifc` show projects with walls, slabs, roofs, stairs, ramps, railings, masses, rooms, shaped floors) — the IFC export itself is not yours, but the saved projects behind those files must come out identical.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

200	## Why BIMCraft
201	
202	- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type
203	  Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO,
204	  RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's
205	  underneath.
206	- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around
207	  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
208	  every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone.
209	- **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with
210	  IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public
211	  specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md):
212	  `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import
213	  its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds
214	  by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read
215	  while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out.
216	- **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to
217	  check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI.
218	- **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on
219	  Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet.
220	- **Free.** MIT OR Apache-2.0, with no account and no subscription.
221	
222	## What works today
223	
224	BIMCraft is in early, fast development. Honest status:
225	
226	| Area | Works today |
227	|---|---|
228	| Datums | Levels with elevations, each a plane over its extent (a rectangle in plan; by default the model's, a metre past it): sections and elevations draw a level where they see its extent, and the 3D view outlines its plane (its far two edges, all four when selected), hidden behind what's in front, its name lettered on a head past the far edges' right end, a click on either picking it; selected, its ends in a section or an elevation and the middles of its plane's edges in 3D are grips that drag its extent; grids that name themselves 1, 2, 3… or A, B, C… |
229	| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
230	| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
231	| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
232	| Ceilings | In the room around a point, out to its walls' faces (Revit's automatic ceiling) and open round any walls standing free inside it (a courtyard's loop, a core), or along a boundary, open through any openings inside it; their underside 2600 mm up by default, their type's thickness over it; types with square tiles, which the reflected ceiling plan draws, stopping at the openings |
233	| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
234	| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
235	| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |

243	| Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. 244	| Types | Wall, floor, ceiling, door, window, column, structural column, footing, beam, strip footing, pipe, conduit, cable tray, wire, down conductor, earthing conductor, cable, roof and railing types; editing one changes every element that uses it (a run type's roundness and material too) |
245	| Materials | A library of materials in each project, as Revit's Material Browser: each with a shading colour, a cut pattern and a surface pattern (solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete or insulation), drawn in code. Plans and sections cut each layer and hatch it with its material's cut pattern where it's wide enough to hold it (a drafting pattern, the same on screen and on paper); a floor's top in plan and a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan show their surface pattern at its size in the building; the 3D view shades each layer in its material's colour. 246	| Editing | Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is); move, copy, rotate and mirror, with the walls joined to them stretching to stay joined and doors and windows going with their walls (a mirrored wall runs back the other way, its exterior mirrored); trim or extend two walls to a corner; split a wall, an arc into two arcs; flip walls; delete (a wall takes its doors and windows with it, and they their tags; a roof or floor walls are attached to lets them go); undo and redo |
247	| Snaps and the ruler | Points picked while drawing stick to what the plan has there, as Revit's snaps do: the ends, middles and centres of walls (an arc's too), grids and components, the centres of columns, structural columns and footings with the corners and edge middles of their outlines (a round one's four quadrants), so a wall can start flush with a column's edge, and the corners of floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; where two straight walls or grids cross; the foot of the perpendicular from the last point to a straight wall or grid; and a wall's centre line, so a wall drawn onto it meets it. It also sticks to the anchors of notes, dimensions, tags, spot elevations, section and elevation marks, detail groups and repeating details; a camera's mark gives its eye and target, never the body, lens or name it is drawn with. Each shows its own marker and its name. A direction from the last point sticks to multiples of an angle (5°, 15°, 30°, 45° or 90°; 15° by default), from east and from the line before it, so corners come out exact, sharp ones too: a dashed guide shows it, and where it crosses a wall or grid the point lands there. The line being drawn carries a ruler: graduations at round lengths, its length and its angle (at the corner it turns once there's a line before it, drawn as an arc). Manage > Snaps switches each snap and sets the angle steps, and Revit's SE, SM, SI, SC, SP and SN take one snap alone for the next point (SO none, SS back); Measure (ME) lays a ruler between two snapped points and reads its length, parts and angle; the `measure` command does the same. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. A viewport takes its view's scale; a sheet keeps annotation at paper size. 284	## Quick start
285	
286	The engine and the CLI need Rust 1.90 or later; the desktop app needs 1.95 (egui 0.36).
287	
288	```sh
289	git clone https://github.com/IPedrax/bimcraft
290	cd bimcraft
291	cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample       # opens the sample house
292	```
293	
294	Without a window:
295	
296	```sh
297	cargo build --release
298	./target/release/bimcraft-cli run --sample --save house.bimcraft --save house.ifc --save plan.png
299	```
300	
301	That builds the sample house and saves the project, an IFC4 file and the Level 1 plan:
302	
303	<p align="center">
304	  <img src="docs/images/sample-plan.png" alt="Level 1 of the sample house: grey wall poché, door swings, windows, its furniture seen from above, room tags with areas, grid bubbles, dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation and a note, and the roof's edge dashed overhead" width="100%">
305	</p>
306	
307	`--cmd 'render {"view": "{3D}", "path": "house-3d.png"}'` adds the 3D view (`azimuth` and `elevation` turn it);
308	`render {"view": "Section 1"}` draws the sample's section, `South` (or `North`, `East`, `West`) one of its elevations, and
309	`render {"view": "A102"}` one of its sheets. `--save sheets.pdf` prints every sheet, a page each.
310	
311	A script is one command per line, `id {json params}`, with lengths in millimetres:
312	
313	```text
314	wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000],[0,6000]], "closed": true, "type": "Exterior - 300mm"}
315	door {"at": [2000, 0]}
316	window {"at": [8000, 3000]}
317	room {"point": [4000, 3000], "name": "Living"}
318	floor {}
319	roof {}

320	```
321	
322	A script stops at its first failing line and names it. Through MCP, `script {"text": …, "atomic": true}` runs it all or nothing:
323	a line that fails takes back the lines before it, and one that goes through is a single undo step.
324	
325	```sh
326	bimcraft-cli run --script house.txt --save house.ifc
327	bimcraft-cli convert building.ifc building.bimcraft   # an IFC file from Revit or any BIM tool, as a project
328	bimcraft-cli info house.bimcraft                      # levels, counts, types and warnings
329	bimcraft-cli info building.rvt                        # a Revit file: release, last save, levels, elements by category
330	bimcraft-cli convert building.rvt building.ifc        # a Revit project, imported, then written as IFC4
331	bimcraft-cli convert house.bimcraft plan.svg
332	bimcraft-cli commands                                 # every command and its parameters
333	```

335	## The desktop app
336	
337	`bimcraft [FILE] [--sample]` opens a `.bimcraft` project, imports an `.ifc` file, or starts on the sample house. The layout
338	is Revit's, so it should feel familiar: the Quick Access Toolbar; the ribbon's File, Architecture, Annotate, View and Modify
339	tabs, with a green contextual tab (Modify | Place Wall, Modify | Walls) for the tool or the selection; the Options Bar;
340	Properties over the Project Browser; views in tabs with a navigation bar; and the tool's prompt in the status bar. The
341	icons and colours are BIMCraft's own: BIMCraft starts in your system's theme. View > Dark Mode opens a menu for Light, Dark,
342	Dark UI, Light Canvas, or As the System; File > Settings offers the same choices. The choice is saved between sessions.
343	
344	Autosave runs in the background every two minutes while the model has unsaved changes (File > Settings > Files changes
345	the interval or disables it). A saved project's recovery copy is `<project filename>.autosave.bimcraft` beside the project;
346	an untitled project's copy is under the system temporary folder's `bimcraft-autosave` directory. Opening a project with a
347	copy offers **Recover**, **Discard**, or **Postpone**. Recover opens unsaved work, Discard removes the copy, and Postpone
348	protects it for later through File > Recover Autosave. Orphaned untitled copies are offered at startup. Successful Save
349	or an explicit Don't Save removes the current recovery copy, except a postponed copy. See [autosave design](docs/autosave.md).
350

The Options Bar sets the height (up to a level, or unconnected), the Location Line (the line of the wall you click along) and Chain. A wall's exterior is to your left as you go, so draw clockwise for walls that face out |

Properties shows their Location Line (pick another and the wall stays where it is) and whether they're attached |

356	| Place rooms | Room (RM), click inside walls; the outline and area show before you click, and the tag's area follows the walls |
357	| Place columns | Column (CL), click where it stands; it snaps to wall ends and centre lines. The Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected), the Type Selector rectangular or round |

421	
422	## Drive it from agents, MCP and the CLI
423	
424	`bimcraft-cli mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio, on a model of its own.
425	Add it to Claude Code:
426	
427	```sh
428	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp
429	```
430	
431	or to any MCP client's configuration:
432	
433	```json
434	{ "mcpServers": { "bimcraft": { "command": "/path/to/bimcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
435	```
436	
437	| Tool | What it does |
438	|---|---|
439	| `execute {command, params}` | Any command with JSON parameters |
440	| `script {text, atomic?}` | Several commands, one per line; `atomic`: all or nothing, one undo step |
441	| `list_commands {filter?}` | The catalog, with parameters and shortcuts |
442	| `inspect_model` | Levels, counts, types, warnings and undo history |
443	| `query_elements {category?, level?}` | Elements with derived values: wall length and height, room area, door position |
444	| `schedule {name?, category?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?}` | A schedule's columns, rows and totals; a new one, or one changed, as the command makes it |
445	| `render {view?, ceiling?, width?, height?, azimuth?, elevation?}` | A level's floor plan (or reflected ceiling plan), a section or elevation by name, a sheet by number, or with `view: "{3D}"` the 3D view, as a PNG the agent can look at |

451	### On the project you have open
452	
453	Start the window with `--control PORT` (`0` for any free port) and an agent can work on the project in front of you instead of
454	a copy of its own: what it makes appears in the window, as an undo step you can take back, and is saved with Ctrl+S.
455	
456	```sh
457	bimcraft --control 0                       # the window says the port; bridge.json beside the favorites holds it and a token
458	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp --connect
459	```
460	
461	`mcp --connect` takes the port from that file (or `--connect PORT` names it, which must be the window's). The port is on this
462	machine's own address only, a connection that does not say the token in its first line is dropped, and only the user can read
463	the file. The tools are the same, except `new_model` and `open`, which would replace your project: start or open another in
464	the window. The window answers between its frames, so a long command holds the window as it would from a button.
465	
466	File > Settings > Agents opens the same port without `--control` (and again at each start), on a port you choose or any free one,
467	and closes it. With **Allow agents to edit this project** off, an agent only reads your project: it inspects it, reads its schedules,
468	renders its views and exports it to new files (the sheets to PDF among them), and every change it asks for comes back as an error
469	that says so. The view control bar shows the port: off, listening on its number, or how many agents are connected, and read-only.
470	An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
471	for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.

689	### Updates
690	
691	The desktop app looks for a newer release when it starts: one HTTPS request to `api.github.com` for this repository's latest
692	release, made on a thread of its own with a 15 second timeout, so the window never waits for it. Being offline, being rate
693	limited, or getting a reply that isn't a release is ignored without a word. It sends nothing of yours beyond what any HTTPS
694	request carries: your address, and a `User-Agent` naming BIMCraft's version (it follows `HTTPS_PROXY` and `ALL_PROXY` like
695	other tools do). A release counts when it's published (not a draft, not a pre-release) and its tag, `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, is
696	a later version than the one running, as semver orders them. A banner then offers it: Update now, Later (it asks again next
697	time), or Skip this version (it stays quiet until a newer one comes). File > Check for Updates Now looks by hand, and says
698	when there's nothing newer or the check failed.
699	
700	The check is switched off in File > Check for updates at startup; that choice is kept in `update.json` beside your
701	favorites, in your own configuration folder (`%APPDATA%\BIMCraft`, `~/Library/Application Support/BIMCraft`, or
702	`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bimcraft`, else `~/.config/bimcraft`; `BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES` moves both), not in a project. Setting the environment variable `BIMCRAFT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` (to anything but empty)
703	keeps the app from making any request, and hides the menu items. `bimcraft-cli` and the MCP server never check for anything.
704	
705	**Windows.** Update now works for the copy the installer put in `Program Files\BIMCraft`; a copy in a folder you picked is
706	told of the new version with a Download button, and the new installer offers that folder again. It downloads
707	`bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64.msi` from the release into a new folder in your temp folder and checks it. Restart and install
708	then asks to save any unsaved changes, closes BIMCraft, and hands over to a copy of itself that waits for BIMCraft to be
709	gone, checks the file once more, runs Windows' own `msiexec` on it while holding the file open, so that nothing can change it
710	(`/passive`: a progress bar, and Windows asks permission, because the installer is for every user) and starts BIMCraft again
711	with the project that was open. If you cancel the permission prompt the old version starts again, and the offer comes back at
712	the next start unless you skipped it. The installer's log is `install.log` in that folder, which BIMCraft removes at a start
713	a day or more later.
714	
715	**Linux.** Update now works for an AppImage whose folder you can write to, on x86_64 or aarch64 (if you start it through a
716	link, the file the link points to is the one replaced). It downloads `bimcraft-<ver>-linux-<arch>.AppImage` into a new folder
717	in your temp folder and checks it. Restart and install then asks to save, checks the file once more, and copies it next to your
718	AppImage under a hidden name, on the same disk, so that the last step can't be left half done. It runs that copy with
719	`--version`, as you would run it and, if that fails (no FUSE, say), once more asking it to unpack itself first, which needs
720	none, giving each try at most a minute; the copy must print `bimcraft <version>` for the release's version. Only then is it
721	renamed over your AppImage, and the new one starts (unpacking itself, if it had to for the check) with the project that was
722	open as BIMCraft closes. The file keeps its name, so a shortcut to it keeps working, even when the name holds the old version.
723	If the new build doesn't run, or says another version, your AppImage is as it was, the hidden copy is deleted and a note says
724	why. A package from your distribution (`.deb`, `.rpm`, Arch) is files that belong to root and to your package manager, so it is
725	told of the newer release and not replaced; so are the tarball, a build from source, and an AppImage in a folder you can't
726	write to. A Flatpak has no network and never checks. None of this has run against a real AppImage: it is tested with scripts
727	that stand in for one, which is what the checks on the new file and the swap need, but not the AppImage runtime itself.
728	
729	**macOS.** Update now works for BIMCraft.app when its folder is one you can write to (Applications, for an administrator, or
730	`~/Applications`). It downloads `bimcraft-<ver>-macos-universal.dmg` into a new folder in your temp folder and checks it.
731	Restart and install then asks to save, checks the file once more, mounts the disk image read-only and out of Finder's sight,
732	copies BIMCraft.app out of it with `ditto` to a hidden app beside yours, lets the image go, and runs `codesign --verify
733	--strict --deep` on the copy, as the release script does. It runs the copy once with `--version`, which must print `bimcraft
734	<version>`, and swaps it in by two renames: the old app is put back if the second fails, and deleted once the new one is in.
735	The new app starts with the project that was open as BIMCraft closes. If a step before the swap fails, your app is as it was, and
736	a note says why; if the new app is in but won't start, the note says that, and BIMCraft stays open. **This has not run on a Mac.** The steps are tested only against shell scripts that stand in for `hdiutil`, `ditto`,
737	`codesign` and `open`, so three things stay open until someone tries it. Whether macOS asks permission, or refuses, when an
738	app signed ad hoc replaces its own bundle (macOS 13 and later guard apps against changes by others; if it refuses, the update
739	fails with that error and the old app stays). Whether Gatekeeper asks again about the new app: it is signed ad hoc like the
740	old one, and the copy BIMCraft makes carries no mark from a download. And whether `open` hands the project to the new app: Finder
741	hands projects over another way, which the app also reads, and if `open` doesn't do it the new version starts with a blank
742	project, while the project is still in the file you saved. An app run from the disk image itself, or from the folder it was
743	downloaded to, can't be replaced (macOS runs a downloaded app from a read-only copy until it is moved): it is told of the newer
744	version and sent to the page, so move BIMCraft to Applications first.
745	
746	**Everything else.** A build from source, a copy kept anywhere else, and a Windows copy running as an administrator are told
747	of a newer release, and the banner's Download button opens its page. Replacing a program that came from `cargo` or a package
748	manager is not the updater's to do, and the copy that runs the Windows installer would have an administrator's rights, in a
749	folder other programs can write to. Run BIMCraft as yourself.
750	
751	**What the check protects against.** The update is fetched only from this repository's release on github.com and GitHub's
752	release CDN, over HTTPS: the address is built from the release's tag, never taken from the reply, redirects are followed one
753	by one and only into this repository's releases on github.com or to the CDN, and an asset is taken only if it's named exactly
754	for that version and kind of install. The reply is read up to 1 MiB, and the download is held to the size GitHub lists for the
755	file (at most 128 MiB) and must match it to the byte. Its SHA-256 must equal the digest GitHub's API gives for that asset, when
756	it arrives and again just before it is installed; and where the release lists a `SHA256SUMS` file, the sum in it must be the
757	same one. The two come from different places (the release workflow writes the file, GitHub works out the digest when an asset is
758	uploaded), so a file replaced afterwards without the other being updated is refused. Nothing runs that failed a check, and the
759	file is deleted. A damaged or truncated download, a cache or a mirror serving something else, and a server that sends more than
760	it should are all stopped by this. On Linux and macOS the new build must also run and say its version before it takes the old
761	one's place, which shows that it loads here, though not that its window opens.
762	
763	**What it doesn't.** None of the three files is signed by a developer identity that BIMCraft checks: the Windows installer isn't
764	code-signed (so Windows can't say who made it), the macOS app is signed ad hoc (which says that it is intact, not who made it),
765	and the AppImage isn't signed. The digest says only that the file is the one GitHub lists: someone who could publish a release
766	in this repository (a stolen token or account), or GitHub itself, would publish a digest that matches their file. On Linux and
767	macOS the new build is run once, as you, with `--version` before it replaces the old one; that is no more trust than starting it
768	after, and the digest check comes first, but it is a program from the internet that runs because you clicked. A program already
769	running as you could swap the file in your temp folder after the first check, and the second check, made just before the install,
770	catches that. On Linux and macOS nothing holds the file between that check and its use, which is a matter of moments, and a
771	program that could win that race could replace your AppImage or your app directly. On Windows the copy that runs the installer
772	holds the file open so that nothing can write to it until Windows Installer is done. If Windows Installer won't open a file held
773	that way, the copy lets go, checks it once more and runs it unheld, and then a swap is possible for as long as you take over the
774	permission prompt, which looks the same either way, since it can't say whose file it is. The updater doesn't mark the file as
775	downloaded from the internet, so SmartScreen doesn't ask as it does for one saved by a browser; the permission prompt still
776	comes from Windows. The certificates it trusts are Mozilla's, built in, so a network that inspects HTTPS with a certificate of
777	its own makes the check fail, quietly, and a corporate root isn't consulted. Signed installers are on the roadmap.

# Levels, walls, roofs, floors, ceilings, shafts, stairs

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the
boundary it has when frozen, both ways it can be measured (`Room::kept`, given after the command that froze it by
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it
and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time
of many rooms; moved, rotated or mirrored, its boundary goes with it, and only a bounded room can be frozen. Walls and columns (and structural columns) bound
rooms while their Room Bounding is on (`Wall::room_bounding`, `Column::room_bounding`, on unless set; `Model::room_bounding`,
`bounding_columns`, `room_lines`): a column's outline either way rooms are measured, a free one an island. A wall with it off
still bounds floors and roofs picked by their walls. Walls and columns bound a level's rooms where its
Computation Height (`Level::computation_height`, 1200 mm unless set) cuts them; room separation lines bound them whatever
it is. Two rooms can't share a space (`Model::room_bound`, `Unbound`): the one placed first (the lower id) keeps it, the
other is unbounded, and `room` and `inspect` warn. A room can be placed where nothing encloses it: unbounded, it covers a
`UNBOUNDED_ROOM` square round its point (`Model::room_outline`), as Revit's. A plan labels it NOT ENCLOSED, or REDUNDANT where another
room has its space. Its reference, a cross from the point it was placed at out along the diagonals to its boundary
(`geom::ray_hit`), drawn as the room's own lines (a click on it picks the room), is the subcategory `roomreference` under
Rooms, off unless shown (`graphics {show: ["roomreference"]}`), beside `roomseparator`, the separation lines.
Subcategories are general (`graphics::SUBCATEGORIES`: a key, its category, a name, whether it is off unless shown):
a view holds them as categories, with `Override::shown` for the ones off unless shown, `Graphics::hides` answers for
them (a category hidden hides its subcategories), and Visibility/Graphics folds them under their category. In a 3D
view rooms are off until shown (`graphics::OFF_IN_3D`, `Graphics::shows_in_3d`; `graphics {view: "{3D}", show: [rooms]}`,
or ticked in its Visibility/Graphics), every new 3D view so; shown, each is drawn as below, fainter than a selected one,
and a selected room is seen whatever the view says: a see-through solid in the selection's colour from its bottom to its top
(`orbit::room_solid`, drawn over the picture, so it shows through walls). With `room_area {at: "finish"}` (`Model::room_area`, Revit's Area and
Volume Computations) room areas are measured at the walls' faces instead (`face_lines` and the separators), the floor inside them; the IFC space
takes that outline, and its `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities` give both whichever is set: `GrossFloorArea` and `GrossPerimeter` at
the centre lines, `NetFloorArea` and `NetPerimeter` at the faces, `Height` (the room's Unbounded Height) and `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`. Walls, slabs, doors and windows
carry theirs too (`ifc::wall_quantities`): a wall its `Length` on its axis, `Width`, `Height` and side and volume, gross and less the
doors and windows in it (each cut to its height; joins aside), or only `Length` and `Width` when attached, as its height then varies;
a level slab its `Width` (depth), `Perimeter` and area and volume less its openings, a sloped one only its `Width`; a door or window
its `Width`, `Height`, `Perimeter` and `Area`. An attached top or base follows the roof's or floor's plane
over each part of the wall (a roof's slopes each over its own part of the plan); a mirrored wall runs back the other way.
A wall's top is `Model::own_top`, and 3D, sections, plans, IFC and what a wall is attached to all read it there (`walls::heights`
takes it, or what the wall is attached to): its `top_level`'s elevation plus its `top_offset` (file format 15, Revit's Top Offset,
mm, negative below the level), or its base plus its `height` when it has no top level, which an offset does not touch.
`Model::check` refuses a wall whose top does not come out above its base, saying how tall it comes out and by how much to raise it.
The Properties palette shows Top Offset under Top Constraint for a wall that has one.
A roof by footprint is the straight skeleton of its outline and its `courtyards` (`skeleton::faces`: the outline
counter-clockwise, the courtyards clockwise, the roof to the left of every edge): each edge moves in at speed 1, a gable's at
0, and its slope rises from it, reaching the roof's base `overhang` in from its eaves; a courtyard's edges number on after
the outline's, and every ring keeps its numbers whichever way round it runs, so `gables` stay put through a mirror.
`Roof::slopes` (file format 15) gives each edge a slope of its own, in degrees, numbered as `gables` are: 0 is the roof's `slope`,
and an empty list, every edge. `Model::roof_faces` then moves an edge in at the run over the rise of its slope, scaled so the
shallowest moves at 1 (every edge at one slope still moves at exactly 1), so edges of different slopes reach the same height
together and the slopes meet along their hips; the eaves stay level, the roof's base `overhang` in from them lowered by the roof's
`slope`, whatever the edges' own. A gable stays upright whatever its slope, and a flat roof (`slope` 0) keeps its `slopes` as it keeps
its `gables`, unused. `Model::check` refuses a list of the wrong length, saying how many edges there are, and a slope outside 0
to 75°, saying which edge. A sketch line may carry a `slope` (`SketchLine::slope`; the Slope row of Properties, with one line of a
roof's sketch picked, sets it): the roof keeps it as the `slopes` of the edges along that line (`sketch::along`), never in its
`sketch`, which `sketch::check` refuses to hold one. `edit_boundary` keeps the slope of an edge that stays or that a new
line cuts in two (an edge lying along an old one), the lines' own `slope` (0 sets the roof's) winning over it, and without
`slope` on the lines it keeps what the edges had; `edit_boundary` without a sketch gives the lines with the slope their edges share.
Over the walls (`floor_outline`, which `roof_footprint` grows by the overhang), a loop of them standing free inside the outer
ones, joined to none of them and with no room in it, is a courtyard, open through the floor and the roof; one joined to them,
or with a room in it, is rooms, and both run over it.
`Model::roof_faces` are its slopes, each the loops round it in plan (a slope can close round a courtyard whose far side is a
gable) with the plane of its underside, trimmed where it `join`s another; `Model::roof_pieces` are those less their holes
and its `openings`, convex where cut. A floor's top is at its level plus `offset`,
or with a slope arrow, there at the arrow's tail and rising `slope` degrees toward its head (`Model::floor_top`); it's its
type's thickness across the slope, so plumb it's thicker. Its `openings` are holes inside it, apart, and `Model::floor_slabs`
what's left, convex where cut. A floor's `shape` (IDEAS MOD-16, [design](../shape-editing.md)) folds its top into planes:
points `z` mm above (negative, below) where the top would be without them, and split lines it folds along, each a part
with an id and a GUID (`ShapePoint`, `SplitLine`). `Model::shape_planes` triangulates its outline, openings, points and
lines (`triangulation::constrained`), lifts each corner by the point there (a corner with none stays at 0) and merges
neighbours in one plane; `Model::floor_faces` are those planes in convex pieces, or the unshaped top, and `floor_slabs`,
the 3D view, sections and the element's details take them. In IFC a shaped slab is one closed `IfcFacetedBrep`
(`Model::shape_solid`: its top's planes, the same planes under them, plumb sides round its outline and openings, each
corner written once), and a sloped or shaped slab gives `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`, its plan through its depth plumb;
every floor's details give `volume_m3`, what's left of it in plan (shafts too) through that depth. A shaped floor is its type's thickness plumb, so its planes meet
underneath too, and has no slope arrow (`Model::check`, `shape_ok`, refuses one, and points outside the outline or in an
opening, points within a millimetre of each other, a split line's end that is no point and no corner, and lines that
cross). A wall attached to one follows `Model::shape_triangles`, its top over the whole outline as if its openings were
closed, as a slope arrow's plane runs on over them. Plans draw each plane's edges as thin as the outline. `edit_shape`
gives the shape anew or says what it is, `add_point`, `add_split_line` and `reset_shape` change it a piece at a time (an
end of a line that is no point becomes one, at the height the top has there), `edit_boundary` keeps what stays inside the
new outline and its openings, cuts a split line where it leaves them, and gives each new end and each new corner a point at
the height the top had there, so a hole cut through a shaped top leaves it as it was round the hole; it names what it
`dropped`, `cut` and `added`. Moves and mirrors take the shape along, and snaps find its points. A flat roof by
footprint (`slope` 0, no extrusion, joining none) takes a shape too (`Roof::shape`, `Roof::unshapeable` says why another
can't): the commands, checks and both views' tools see its top as a floor's (`Model::shapeable`, `Model::roof_as_floor`:
its footprint, its courtyards and openings as openings, at its top), and `roof_faces` lays each plane's underside its
thickness below, plumb (`roof_rise`), so its slabs, IFC, sections and the walls attached under it follow its falls; plans
draw its creases thin. Under its type's variable layer a shaped roof's underside stays level at its base
(`Model::roof_under`, `roof_prisms`), as a floor's does: its layers in 3D and sections share `Variable::bounds` through
`Model::variable_under`, walls attached under it stop at that underside, IFC writes it as one closed faceted Brep
(`Model::roof_solid`), and `Model::check` refuses a point that leaves the layer thinner than nothing. `falls` (`falls.rs`) gives a floor or a flat roof its shape from its drains and the least fall:
catchments nearest each drain, ridges between them at the top's height, valleys from each drain to its catchment's corners,
each drain as deep as the fall takes its farthest corner; round an opening the valleys turn at its corners, which lie on
the drain's cone, and ridges drawn part the top first. A slab or flat roof whose top isn't one plane comes in from IFC
shaped (`import::shaped_top`), its variable layer marked by its `Description` or, under a level underside, guessed
(`import::guess_variable`); and a spot slope (`Spot::slope`) reads a floor's or roof's fall in a plan. A layer of a floor or roof type may be `variable` (one a type at most; never a wall's or a ceiling's): under a
shaped floor of that type, the underside stays level where the unshaped floor's was (`Model::floor_under`), the layers
above the variable one follow the top, those below it stay level, and the variable one takes up the difference
(`Variable::bounds`, which the 3D view's layers and sections share). Its pieces are then prisms from that level underside
(`Model::floor_prisms`), its volume is less where its top falls (`Model::floor_volume`, `model::volume` for IFC), a wall
attached under it stops at the level underside, and `Model::check` refuses a point that would leave the variable layer
thinner than nothing, saying by how much to raise it. Reinforcement arms a shaped floor only when a variable layer lies
over all its structure: the bars keep to the layers under it, as on a level floor that thick. Without one it refuses,
saying why. In the desktop, a floor selected shows Shape Editing in its contextual tab: Slope Arrow, Modify Sub Elements (a point, a corner or an edge's two ends,
`Floor::shape_pick`, to the Options Bar's Elevation), Add Point (a
click on the top, at the Options Bar's Elevation, above the unshaped top or, with Absolute, above the level; empty, the
top's height there), Add Split Line (two clicks, snapping to points, corners and edges) and Reset Shape, each a command.
While one is on, each point's height is labelled beside it (`Model::shape_labels`); under Modify Sub Elements a point's
grip drags it in plan at its height, its split lines with it (`Shape::moved`), in one `edit_shape`. In the 3D view the
same tools work on the floor's top: each point's and corner's grip drags its height up or down, and clicks land on the top
(`view3d::shape_handles`, `on_floor_top`, `shape_pick_3d`); both views run `shape.rs`. While a grip is held, either
view draws the creases its release will leave (`Model::shape_creases` of the floor with the shape it would have). Type Properties ticks a floor's or a roof's variable layer. A ceiling's `offset` is its underside; its `openings` are holes as a floor's
are, and `Model::ceiling_slabs` what's left. A shaft cuts each floor,
ceiling and roof its span reaches into over its outline, all the way through (`Model::less_shafts`). A stair or a ramp
is runs and landings laid out from its start (`stairs::stair`, `stairs::ramp`): a landing after `at` risers (a ramp's, `at`
mm up), as deep as the runs are wide, the next run turning by its `turn`; a railing on one follows its walk line moved out to
its side (`stairs::railing`), so it goes wherever its host goes. `modify` merges into fields that are objects (JSON Merge Patch), so `{"view_range": {"cut": 1500}}` keeps the rest; an element's own field can't be
called `category`, the tag every element carries.

Sketches (`sketch.rs`) are how an outline is drawn, the one solver everything with an outline and holes uses: floors,
ceilings, roofs by footprint, shafts and filled regions now, topography next. A sketch is `SketchLine`s, straight or
arcs (a point `through`), in any order, either way round; `sketch::solve` cuts arcs into chords no more than 5° round,
welds ends within `TOL`, then names every problem at once with the lines it's about, what to fix first first
(`Problem::rank`: a line too short or out of range; two lines crossing, or one ending part way along another; two along
each other; three or more at a point; an end no other meets; a loop with no area), and otherwise walks the loops and nests
them by how many others each is inside: even, an outline (counter-clockwise), odd, a hole (clockwise) of the innermost loop
round it, so an island in a hole is an outline again. `solve_one` wants one outline (a floor's, a roof's). The element
keeps the sketch it was drawn or last edited by (`sketch` on floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; empty when it was made
over the walls or read from a file): each line is a part with an id and a GUID of its own (`HasPart`, listed in
`parts_now` by the element's GUID), going with the element when it moves and new on a copy; part ids are not given
again once a line is gone, for as long as the project is open (the library remembers the lowest it has held; a file holds the
ids in use, so one a line had before it was deleted and the file saved may be given again after the file is reopened). Commands take `sketch` (lines `[[x,y],[x,y]]`, arcs `[[x,y],[x,y],[x,y]]`, or
`{start, end, through?, id?}`) in place of `boundary` and its holes; `edit_boundary` without one gives the lines to edit
(the kept sketch while it still draws the outline, `sketch::draws`, else the outline's edges as new lines) and with one
redraws it, a line sent back with its `id` keeping it (keeping a roof's gables on edges that stay); the `sketch` command
solves without making anything. Messages name a line by its id, or its place in the list while it has none. A boundary
given as points is cleaned (a repeated point dropped, and one within a millimetre of the last), and every outline a command
makes or changes, whichever command (`floor`, `modify`, `edit_boundary`, `move`…), is judged as the sketch of its edges
(`Model::check_edits`, asked by the engine after each command but Insert from File): a floor's, ceiling's or roof's boundary,
an opening or a courtyard, a shaft's boundary, that crosses itself or lies along itself, has an edge ending part way along
another, or a spike or keyhole slit, is refused, saying which edges and where, and what to do: redraw it with `edit_boundary`; give
`boundary` or `sketch` (with the walls that touch at a corner named only when it was taken from walls), or simple `openings` or
`courtyards` for one of those rings, for one a command was making;
redraw the mass whose outline it is, for one made by face or by `mass_floors` (a mass itself may still have a bow tie outline,
a spike or a corner touching an edge, so the message says the outline isn't simple, not that it crosses itself);
and, for a roof's opening, which `edit_boundary` does not edit, give `modify` a simple `openings`, and from `dormer` change the
dormer's width, height or position. That is a change from the base, which let
`modify` and the commands that weren't given points set such an outline. `Model::check` doesn't judge the whole project by
it: a file, an IFC import or a Revit import with a keyhole outline still opens, and what leaves its outline alone (`modify`
of its offset, `delete`, `edit_boundary` with a sketch that is simple) still works, and so does what moves, copies, turns or mirrors
it, which makes it no worse (a copy is judged against the elements the command was given, so a new floor drawn with a bow tie
the file also holds is refused); what changes its shape is asked to redraw it first. One line that crosses itself (a closed polyline round a bow tie, a spline with a loop) is found as two lines
crossing are, and a sketch is refused at once past 200,000 straight pieces (a circle is up to 8,193 of them), or when its
pieces lie so close together that telling which cross would take six million steps.

The desktop's sketch mode (`crates/ui-egui/src/sketch.rs`) holds the lines until Finish Edit Mode, which solves them
first and says what's wrong for whoever drew it (`sketch::friendly`: what to fix, kind by kind, where, in the project's
units, and the lines by id) with those lines in the error colour; solved, it runs the command. Draw has every shape of
the Draw panel (`draw.rs`; lines, rectangles, polygons, circles, the arcs, Fillet Arc on two sketch lines, splines, ellipses,
polylines, Pick Lines: see [views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)) and Pick Walls (a line along each wall's location
line, an arc along an arc wall); a sketch line is any curve, so a circle or an ellipse is a loop of its own. Modify picks
sketch lines (a click, a window box from the left, a crossing box from the right), a picked line's handles (its corners, a
spline's points, a circle's centre) are grips that take every one joined there with them, and Delete removes them; Ctrl+Z takes back a line; the plan's snaps take the
sketch's own ends, middles, crossings and curves as well as visible view-specific detail (`snap::in_sketch`). Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft each start a new one (Boundary
Line, Sketch Ceiling); Edit Boundary redraws one selected. The Mode panel (Finish, Cancel; Edit Boundary) stands at the
ribbon's right end.

What the line tools hold to, and don't (`curves.rs`, `draw.rs`, `sketch.rs`). A curve is drawn as chords none further than `FLAT`
(0.25 mm) from it: a polyline's arcs, a circle, a spline and a fitted spline (a span of a spline is cut by the greatest
second derivative on it, so a ten metre arch is hundreds of chords), up to `MAX_DRAWN` extra points in all; a polyline whose
arcs would take more is refused, and a circle past about 3.4 km of radius (`MAX_DRAWN` chords stray `FLAT` from it there) is drawn coarser than `FLAT` rather than in more, 0.37 mm off at 5 km and 2 mm off at 27 km.
An arc, a circle or an ellipse reaches no further than `MAX_COORD` from the origin, as a wall's arc must; a spline lies inside
its control points, and a fitted spline is held to its points only, a cubic through them straying a little past. A curve's
start and end are the points it was given. Offset moves a polyline's lines along themselves and its arcs about their own
centres and makes each corner where the moved sides cross; it gives nothing where a side would vanish or turn round, or a
corner is so sharp its mitre would be 50 offsets long, and it does not trim a fold it makes in a concave shape (Revit's
does); an ellipse or a spline offsets to a fitted spline within 0.05 mm. Fillet on walls keeps their doors and windows
where they stand and refuses to cut one off, but does not stretch a third wall that ended on the corner. A detail line with
no style gets Thin Lines by the project's name, else the English one, else the thin black solid style. Of the line tools,
Revit has default shortcuts for Trim/Extend to Corner (TR), Offset (OF), Fillet (FL), Split (SL) and Detail Line (DL), which
`corner`, `offset`, `fillet`, `split` and `detail_line` have; it has none for Trim/Extend to a boundary, vertices, Convert
Spline, Edit Boundary, line patterns and styles or fill patterns, which have none here. Explode Polyline is EX, ours (PX is
the desktop's Plumbing Fixture).
