def sub(a,b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1])
def cross(a,b): return a[0]*b[1]-a[1]*b[0]
def dot(a,b): return a[0]*b[0]+a[1]*b[1]
def circum(a,b,c):
    ax,ay=a; bx,by=b; cx,cy=c
    d = 2*(ax*(by-cy)+bx*(cy-ay)+cx*(ay-by))
    ux = ((ax*ax+ay*ay)*(by-cy)+(bx*bx+by*by)*(cy-ay)+(cx*cx+cy*cy)*(ay-by))/d
    uy = ((ax*ax+ay*ay)*(cx-bx)+(bx*bx+by*by)*(ax-cx)+(cx*cx+cy*cy)*(bx-ax))/d
    return (ux,uy)
def circum2(a,b,c):
    # relative to a
    bx,by = b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]; cx,cy = c[0]-a[0], c[1]-a[1]
    d = 2*(bx*cy-by*cx)
    ux = (cy*(bx*bx+by*by)-by*(cx*cx+cy*cy))/d
    uy = (bx*(cx*cx+cy*cy)-cx*(bx*bx+by*by))/d
    return (a[0]+ux, a[1]+uy)
for a,b,t,exp in cases:
    res = {}
    ta, tb = sub(a,t), sub(b,t)
    ang = math.atan2(cross(ta,tb), dot(ta,tb))
    res['2(pi-|ang|)sign'] = math.copysign(2*(math.pi-abs(ang)), -ang)
    res['deg 2(pi-|ang|)'] = math.degrees(2*(math.pi-abs(ang)))
    res['deg 2pi-2|ang|'] = math.degrees(2*math.pi-2*abs(ang))
    res['deg 360-2|angdeg|'] = 360 - 2*abs(math.degrees(ang))
    for cn, cf in (('circ', circum), ('circ2', circum2)):
        c = cf(a,b,t)
        a0 = math.atan2(a[1]-c[1], a[0]-c[0]); a1 = math.atan2(b[1]-c[1], b[0]-c[0]); at = math.atan2(t[1]-c[1], t[0]-c[0])
        # ccw sweep from a0 to a1
        sw = (a1 - a0) % (2*math.pi)
        st = (at - a0) % (2*math.pi)
        if st > sw: sw = sw - 2*math.pi
        res[cn+' deg(sw)'] = math.degrees(sw)
        res[cn+' sw*180/pi'] = sw*180/math.pi
    for k, v in res.items():

def orig(line):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(d, 's.txt'), 'w').write(line + '\n')
    p = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable', 'run', '--script', 's.txt'], cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    return json.loads(p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1])
o = orig('sketch {"lines": [{"centre": [0,0], "radius": 1000}]}')
pts = o['regions'][0]['outline']
n = len(pts)
print('n', n)
r = 1000.0
tau = 2*math.pi
forms = {
  'tau*i/n': lambda i: tau*i/n,
  'i*(tau/n)': lambda i: i*(tau/n),
  'tau*(i/n)': lambda i: tau*(i/n),
  'rad(360*i/n)': lambda i: math.radians(360.0*i/n),
  'rad(i*(360/n))': lambda i: math.radians(i*(360.0/n)),
  '2pi*i/n': lambda i: 2*math.pi*i/n,
  'pi*2i/n': lambda i: math.pi*(2*i)/n,
  'i/n*tau': lambda i: i/n*tau,
}
step = tau/n
acc = [0.0]
for i in range(n): acc.append(acc[-1]+step)
forms['acc'] = lambda i: acc[i]
for name, f in forms.items():
    ok = sum(1 for i in range(n) if (r*math.cos(f(i)), r*math.sin(f(i))) == tuple(pts[i]))
    ok2 = sum(1 for i in range(n) if (0.0 + r*math.cos(f(i)), 0.0 + r*math.sin(f(i))) == tuple(pts[i]))
    print(name, ok, ok2)
# rotation incremental
co, si = math.cos(step), math.sin(step)
x, y = r, 0.0
ok = 0
for i in range(n):
    if (x, y) == tuple(pts[i]): ok += 1
    x, y = x*co - y*si, x*si + y*co
print('incrot', ok)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

doors and windows in it (each cut to its height; joins aside), or only `Length` and `Width` when attached, as its height then varies;
a level slab its `Width` (depth), `Perimeter` and area and volume less its openings, a sloped one only its `Width`; a door or window
its `Width`, `Height`, `Perimeter` and `Area`. An attached top or base follows the roof's or floor's plane
over each part of the wall (a roof's slopes each over its own part of the plan); a mirrored wall runs back the other way.
A wall's top is `Model::own_top`, and 3D, sections, plans, IFC and what a wall is attached to all read it there (`walls::heights`
takes it, or what the wall is attached to): its `top_level`'s elevation plus its `top_offset` (file format 15, Revit's Top Offset,
mm, negative below the level), or its base plus its `height` when it has no top level, which an offset does not touch.
`Model::check` refuses a wall whose top does not come out above its base, saying how tall it comes out and by how much to raise it.
The Properties palette shows Top Offset under Top Constraint for a wall that has one.
A roof by footprint is the straight skeleton of its outline and its `courtyards` (`skeleton::faces`: the outline
counter-clockwise, the courtyards clockwise, the roof to the left of every edge): each edge moves in at speed 1, a gable's at
0, and its slope rises from it, reaching the roof's base `overhang` in from its eaves; a courtyard's edges number on after
the outline's, and every ring keeps its numbers whichever way round it runs, so `gables` stay put through a mirror.
`Roof::slopes` (file format 15) gives each edge a slope of its own, in degrees, numbered as `gables` are: 0 is the roof's `slope`,
and an empty list, every edge. `Model::roof_faces` then moves an edge in at the run over the rise of its slope, scaled so the
shallowest moves at 1 (every edge at one slope still moves at exactly 1), so edges of different slopes reach the same height
together and the slopes meet along their hips; the eaves stay level, the roof's base `overhang` in from them lowered by the roof's
`slope`, whatever the edges' own. A gable stays upright whatever its slope, and a flat roof (`slope` 0) keeps its `slopes` as it keeps
its `gables`, unused. `Model::check` refuses a list of the wrong length, saying how many edges there are, and a slope outside 0
to 75°, saying which edge. A sketch line may carry a `slope` (`SketchLine::slope`; the Slope row of Properties, with one line of a
roof's sketch picked, sets it): the roof keeps it as the `slopes` of the edges along that line (`sketch::along`), never in its
`sketch`, which `sketch::check` refuses to hold one. `edit_boundary` keeps the slope of an edge that stays or that a new
line cuts in two (an edge lying along an old one), the lines' own `slope` (0 sets the roof's) winning over it, and without
`slope` on the lines it keeps what the edges had; `edit_boundary` without a sketch gives the lines with the slope their edges share.

ones, joined to none of them and with no room in it, is a courtyard, open through the floor and the roof; one joined to them,
or with a room in it, is rooms, and both run over it.
`Model::roof_faces` are its slopes, each the loops round it in plan (a slope can close round a courtyard whose far side is a

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run a fl.py-style group file on both and diff the boundaries point by point."""
import sys, json
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/arch-agent')
import fl
groups = []
cur = []
for l in open(sys.argv[1]).read().split('\n'):
    if not l.strip():
        if cur: groups.append(cur); cur = []
    else:
        cur.append(l)
if cur: groups.append(cur)
key = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 'boundary'
for g in groups:
    o = fl.run(g, fl.ORIG, keys=(key,))
    m = fl.run(g, fl.MINE, keys=(key,))
    def pts(s):
        for line in s.split('\n'):
            line = line.strip()
            if ' %s=' % key in line:
                return json.loads(line.split(' %s=' % key, 1)[1])
        return None
    po, pm = pts(o), pts(m)
    print('==', ' | '.join(g))
    if po is None or pm is None:
        print('  O:', o[:300]); print('  M:', m[:300]); continue
    if len(po) != len(pm):
        print('  len', len(po), len(pm))
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(po, pm)):

another, or a spike or keyhole slit, is refused, saying which edges and where, and what to do: redraw it with `edit_boundary`; give
`boundary` or `sketch` (with the walls that touch at a corner named only when it was taken from walls), or simple `openings` or
`courtyards` for one of those rings, for one a command was making;
redraw the mass whose outline it is, for one made by face or by `mass_floors` (a mass itself may still have a bow tie outline,
a spike or a corner touching an edge, so the message says the outline isn't simple, not that it crosses itself);
and, for a roof's opening, which `edit_boundary` does not edit, give `modify` a simple `openings`, and from `dormer` change the
dormer's width, height or position. That is a change from the base, which let
`modify` and the commands that weren't given points set such an outline. `Model::check` doesn't judge the whole project by
it: a file, an IFC import or a Revit import with a keyhole outline still opens, and what leaves its outline alone (`modify`
of its offset, `delete`, `edit_boundary` with a sketch that is simple) still works, and so does what moves, copies, turns or mirrors
it, which makes it no worse (a copy is judged against the elements the command was given, so a new floor drawn with a bow tie

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fit the original's arc tessellation: sketch a closed shape of a line and an arc, collect the
outline points, and test formulas for the interior points.
usage: arcfit.py ax ay bx by deg"""
import json, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os, shutil, math, itertools
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
def run(exe, lines):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(d, 's.txt'), 'w').write('\n'.join(lines) + '\n')
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'run', '--script', 's.txt'], cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1]
ax, ay, bx, by, deg = [float(x) for x in sys.argv[1:6]]
cmd = 'sketch {"lines": [{"start": [%r,%r], "end": [%r,%r]}, {"start": [%r,%r], "end": [%r,%r], "arc": %r}]}' % (bx, by, ax, ay, ax, ay, bx, by, deg)
o = json.loads(run(ORIG, [cmd]))
if 'regions' not in o:
    print(o); sys.exit()
pts = o['regions'][0]['outline']
S = set(tuple(p) for p in pts)
S.discard((ax, ay)); S.discard((bx, by))
n = len(S) + 1
print('n chords', n, 'pts', len(pts))
PI = math.pi
def rad(d): return d * (PI / 180.0)
a = (ax, ay); b = (bx, by)
def centres():
    sw = rad(deg)
    ch = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])
    c = math.hypot(*ch)
    h = sw / 2
    mid = ((a[0]+b[0])*0.5, (a[1]+b[1])*0.5)
    mid2 = (a[0] + ch[0]*0.5, a[1] + ch[1]*0.5)
    u = (ch[0]/c, ch[1]/c)
    l = (-u[1], u[0])
    out = {}
    for mn, m in [('mid', mid), ('mid2', mid2)]:
        for dn, d in [('c/2/tan', c/2/math.tan(h)), ('c/(2tan)', c/(2*math.tan(h))), ('r*cos', (c/2/abs(math.sin(h)))*math.cos(h)*(1 if h>0 else -1))]:
            out[mn+','+dn] = (m[0] + l[0]*d, m[1] + l[1]*d)
    return out
sw = rad(deg)
ch = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]); c = math.hypot(*ch); h = sw/2
for cname, C in centres().items():
    for rname, r in [('c/2/|sin|', c/2/abs(math.sin(h))), ('dist', math.hypot(a[0]-C[0], a[1]-C[1])), ('c/(2|sin|)', c/(2*abs(math.sin(h))))]:
        a0 = math.atan2(a[1]-C[1], a[0]-C[0])
        a1 = math.atan2(b[1]-C[1], b[0]-C[0])
        angs = {
            'a0+sw*i/n': lambda i: a0 + sw*i/n,
            'a0+sw*(i/n)': lambda i: a0 + sw*(i/n),
            'a0+(sw/n)*i': lambda i: a0 + (sw/n)*i,
            'a0+rad(deg*i/n)': lambda i: a0 + rad(deg*i/n),
            'a0+i*sw/n': lambda i: a0 + i*sw/n,
        }
        for an, af in angs.items():
            for fn in ['C+r*cs', 'C+cs*r']:
                got = set()
                for i in range(1, n):
                    t = af(i)
                    if fn == 'C+r*cs':
                        q = (C[0] + r*math.cos(t), C[1] + r*math.sin(t))
                    else:
                        q = (C[0] + math.cos(t)*r, C[1] + math.sin(t)*r)
                    got.add(q)
                bad = len(S - got)
                if bad <= 2:
                    print('%-16s %-11s %-16s %-7s bad %d' % (cname, rname, an, fn, bad))
print('done')

ax, ay, bx, by, deg = [float(x) for x in sys.argv[1:6]]

            out[mn+','+dn] = (m[0] + l[0]*d, m[1] + l[1]*d)

ch = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]); c = math.hypot(*ch); h = sw/2

import json, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os, shutil, math
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
def run(exe, lines):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(d, 's.txt'), 'w').write('\n'.join(lines) + '\n')
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'run', '--script', 's.txt'], cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1]
def orig_arc(ax, ay, bx, by, deg):
    cmd = 'sketch {"lines": [{"start": [%r,%r], "end": [%r,%r]}, {"start": [%r,%r], "end": [%r,%r], "arc": %r}]}' % (bx, by, ax, ay, ax, ay, bx, by, deg)
    o = json.loads(run(ORIG, [cmd]))
    pts = [tuple(p) for p in o['regions'][0]['outline']]
    a = (ax, ay); b = (bx, by)
    k = pts.index(a)
    pts = pts[k:] + pts[:k]
    if pts[1] == b:
        pts = [pts[0]] + list(reversed(pts[1:]))
    return pts  # a, interior..., b
PI = math.pi
def rad(d): return d * (PI / 180.0)
def variants(a, b, deg, n):
    sw = rad(deg)
    ch = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]); c = math.hypot(*ch); h = sw/2
    mid = ((a[0]+b[0])*0.5, (a[1]+b[1])*0.5)
    u = (ch[0]/c, ch[1]/c); l = (-u[1], u[0])
    out = {}
    for dn, d in [('d=c/2/tan', c/2/math.tan(h)), ('d=c/2*cos/sin', c/2*math.cos(h)/math.sin(h)), ('d=r*cos', (c/2/math.sin(h))*math.cos(h))]:
        C = (mid[0] + l[0]*d, mid[1] + l[1]*d)
        for rn, r in [('r=c/2/sin', c/2/abs(math.sin(h))), ('r=dist', math.hypot(a[0]-C[0], a[1]-C[1]))]:
            a0 = math.atan2(a[1]-C[1], a[0]-C[0])
            a1 = math.atan2(b[1]-C[1], b[0]-C[0])
            def polar(t): return (C[0] + r*math.cos(t), C[1] + r*math.sin(t))
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar a0+rad(deg*i/n)'] = [polar(a0 + rad(deg*i/n)) for i in range(n+1)]
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar a0+sw*i/n'] = [polar(a0 + sw*i/n) for i in range(n+1)]
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar a0+rad(deg/n*i)'] = [polar(a0 + rad(deg/n*i)) for i in range(n+1)]
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar a0+rad(deg)*i/n'] = [polar(a0 + rad(deg)*i/n) for i in range(n+1)]
            v = (a[0]-C[0], a[1]-C[1])
            def rot(t):
                cs, sn = math.cos(t), math.sin(t)
                return (C[0] + v[0]*cs - v[1]*sn, C[1] + v[0]*sn + v[1]*cs)
            out[dn+' '+rn+' rot rad(deg*i/n)'] = [rot(rad(deg*i/n)) for i in range(n+1)]
            out[dn+' '+rn+' rot sw*i/n'] = [rot(sw*i/n) for i in range(n+1)]
            # angles via lerp between a0 and a0+sw
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar lerp'] = [polar(a0 + (a0+sw - a0)*i/n) for i in range(n+1)]
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar a0*(1-t)+a1t'] = [polar(a0*(1-i/n) + (a0+sw)*(i/n)) for i in range(n+1)]
            # start angle in degrees
            a0d = math.degrees(a0)
            out[dn+' '+rn+' polar rad(a0d+deg*i/n)'] = [polar(rad(a0d + deg*i/n)) for i in range(n+1)]
    return out
args = [float(x) for x in sys.argv[1:6]]
pts = orig_arc(*args)
n = len(pts) - 1
a = (args[0], args[1]); b = (args[2], args[3])
res = []
for name, q in variants(a, b, args[4], n).items():
    bad = sum(1 for i in range(1, n) if q[i] != pts[i])
    res.append((bad, name))
res.sort()
for bad, name in res[:8]:
    print(bad, name)
print('n', n)

python3 -c "
import math
def unit(v):
    l = math.hypot(*v); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
def left(v): return (-v[1], v[0])
def solve(n1, c1, n2, c2):
    det = n1[0]*n2[1] - n1[1]*n2[0]
    return ((c1*n2[1] - c2*n1[1])/det, (n1[0]*c2 - n2[0]*c1)/det)
W = [((0.,0.),(3000.,1000.)), ((3000.,1000.),(500.,4000.)), ((500.,4000.),(0.,0.))]
def line(w, side=0.0):
    a, b = w
    n = left(unit((b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])))
    return n, n[0]*a[0] + n[1]*a[1] + side
def line_b(w):
    a, b = w
    n = left(unit((b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])))
    return n, n[0]*b[0] + n[1]*b[1]
for i in range(3):
    j = (i+1)%3
    n1,c1 = line(W[i]); n2,c2 = line(W[j])
    print('corner', W[i][1], 'A', solve(n1,c1,n2,c2), 'B', solve(n2,c2,n1,c1))
    n1,c1 = line_b(W[i]); n2,c2 = line(W[j])
    print('      b-end', solve(n1,c1,n2,c2), solve(n2,c2,n1,c1))
print('want (500, 3999.9999999999995) (3000, 1000.0000000000001)')
"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""craft.py base.bimcraft 'python statements on d (the doc) and E (elements dict by int id)' [command]
Writes a crafted copy, opens it with the original (and mine with -b), runs a trivial command, prints the result."""
import json, sys, subprocess, tempfile, os, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-aa380c34464cd9919/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
args = sys.argv[1:]
both = False
if args and args[0] == '-b':
    both = True
    args = args[1:]
base, code = args[0], args[1]
cmd = args[2] if len(args) > 2 else 'level {"elevation": 90000}'
d = json.load(open(base))
E = {int(k): v for k, v in d['elements'].items()}
def guid(i):
    return E[i]['guid']
exec(code)
d['elements'] = {str(k): v for k, v in sorted(E.items())}
def run(exe):
    t = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    json.dump(d, open(os.path.join(t, 'c.bimcraft'), 'w'), indent=2)
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'run', 'c.bimcraft', '--cmd', cmd], cwd=t, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(t)
    return (p.stdout.decode() + p.stderr.decode()).strip()
o = run(ORIG)
print('O:', o)
if both:
    m = run(MINE)
    print('M:', m)
    print('SAME' if m == o else 'DIFF')

## wall ['WA'] Wall
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

## door ['DR'] Door
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

## window ['WN'] Window
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

## floor [] Floor
{boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline

## ceiling [] Ceiling
{point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it

## sketch [] Sketch
{lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about (numbered from 0): ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line too: a polyline round a bow tie crosses itself), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc, a circle or a curve is cut into chords, a circle into up to 8,193): past 200,000 of them, or when they lie so close together that telling which cross takes more than six million steps, it is refused at once. `sketch` on floor, ceiling, roof and shaft, and edit_boundary, take the same lines for one outline and its holes

## shaft [] Shaft Opening
{boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`

## edit_boundary [] Edit Boundary
{id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The outline must be simple, as `floor` says; a line that crosses itself is found as two that cross are

## edit_shape [] Modify Sub Elements
{id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height the top has there. Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)

## add_point [] Add Point
{id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height

## add_split_line [] Add Split Line
{id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now

## reset_shape [] Reset Shape
{id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again

## falls [] Falls
{id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain

## mass ['MS'] Mass
{boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`

## mass_floors ['MF'] Mass Floors
{mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level

## wall_by_face ['WB'] Wall by Face
{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

## floor_by_face ['FB'] Floor by Face
{mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on

## roof_by_face ['RB'] Roof by Face
{mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on

## update_by_face ['UF'] Update to Face
{mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`

## show_mass ['MH'] Show Mass
{view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's

## room ['RM'] Room
{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

## room_separator [] Room Separator
{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

## stair [] Stair
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too

## ramp [] Ramp
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level

## railing [] Railing
{host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are

## roof [] Roof
{level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over `boundary` or else the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces, round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it): flat at `slope` 0, else every edge sloping up at `slope` degrees (30), hips, valleys and ridges where the slopes meet, but the edges in `gables` (edge i runs from point i to the next, the courtyards' edges numbered on after the boundary's) left upright, gable ends; `gable` leaves a rectangle's short ends upright. `slopes`: a slope in degrees (up to 75) for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for an edge that takes `slope`; none, every edge does; the eaves stay level and an edge in `gables` stays upright whatever its slope. A `sketch` line may carry a `slope` for the edges along it. Or with `extrusion` {line: [[x,y],[x,y]], profile: [[along, up],…], from?, to}: its underside's profile in the upright plane through `line`, along it from its start and up from the base, swept square to it from `from` (0) to `to` mm to its left. `openings` are holes through it in plan; with `join`, a roof it runs into, it ends where it meets that one's top

## dormer [] Dormer
{host, at: [x, y], width?, height?, slope?, window?, type?} a dormer on roof `host`, its front wall across the slope through `at`: walls of `type` `width` mm (1600) apart, standing on the roof and `height` mm (1200) tall at the front, under a gable roof of its own sloping `slope` degrees (30) that runs back into the host; the host open under it, and with `window` (a window type) a window in its front. Replies with its roof, walls and window

## flip [] Flip
{ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

content.content:
# Levels, walls, roofs, floors, ceilings, shafts, stairs

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the

# Masses

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

A mass (`Mass`, category `mass`) is a footprint (`Mass::footprint`: counter-clockwise whichever way `boundary` runs) extruded from
`base_offset` over `level` up to `top_level` or `height`, as a shaft is, with `params`. Given a `top` outline (as many points as
`boundary`, twin for twin, and running the same way round; `Mass::top_ring` has it counter-clockwise like the footprint) it is lofted
straight between the two (`Mass::lofted`: a `top` equal to the footprint is no loft, and the `mass` command drops it; its `lean`
parameter makes `top` by moving the footprint sideways, a sloped mass). `Model::mass_outline(ms, z)` is the cross section at a height,
the footprint, or each corner that far along its way to its twin (`massing::ring_at`), and everything that measures a mass asks it:
floors, the `massfloor` and `mass` schedules, gross floor area, the plan, snaps. The area is a quadratic of the height, so
`Model::mass_volume` is Simpson's rule on three cross sections, exact. `massing::loft_problem` (which `Model::check` and the IFC import
both ask) refuses a top outline that doesn't pair up, runs the other way round, or collapses the cross section at some sixteenth of
the way up. A plan dashes the outline at its cut height where the plane passes through it (`Model::mass_cut_by`); a section outlines
where its line cuts it and never fills it in poché (`section` leaves masses out of `cuts`; a straight one's stretches come from
`view3d::crossings`, a lofted one's lines from `massing::section_lines`, the cut of its skin of triangles, joined end to end); 3D draws
a straight one as a slab and a lofted one as `massing::tris`, a closed skin turned out (two triangles on a side whose twin
edges are parallel, which makes it flat; a side that twists is cut into `massing::STRIPS` strips up its height, so a twisted loft's volume
in 3D and IFC is a percent or two under the exact one, while the areas and volumes the model reports are exact),
see-through by `graphics::MASS_TRANSPARENCY` unless the view's graphics say otherwise (`Look::with` starts a mass's override there, so a
project with masses never takes its plain shortcut). Show Mass (`show_mass`, MH) is `graphics {hide|show: [mass]}` on one view.
`Model::mass_slices` is the levels it crosses, from its base up to, not including, its top, each with how far the mass goes up from
there: `mass_floors` and the rows of the `massfloor` schedule (`schedule::sources`; a `Row` carries the schedule's category, not its
element's) come from it.
What a mass makes remembers it, under reserved names in `params` as phases and paint are held (`massing.rs`; no project or family
parameter may take them, `Model::check` holds each to a real mass and a level or a face of the right kind, `delete` takes off the marks
naming a mass that goes, and a copy or a split piece loses its own). `mass_floors` leaves `Mass Floor`, `{mass, level}`, on its floors,
so a second run finds them by it, gives them the mass's outline at their level (and the type, if one is given), makes none again, lists
as `stale` the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses and deletes those only with `prune`. `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and
`roof_by_face` build their element by running `wall`, `floor` and `roof` with the face's parameters, so those commands' checks stay the
one place, and leave `Mass Face`, `{mass, face}`: an edge number (numbered from the first point, counter-clockwise) for a wall, `"top"`
for a floor or a roof. A wall stands plumb, so only on a face whose top edge is right over its bottom edge (`massing::plumb`); a floor
and a roof lie on the top outline. `update_by_face` (UF; Revit's Update to Face has no default shortcut) rebuilds the geometry of the
ones asked for, a mass's, or all of them (`massing::follow`: a wall's ends, level, offset and height or top level; a floor's or roof's
boundary, level and offset; the type, a roof's slope and the rest stay) and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. A mass
mirrored in place runs its outline round the other way, so `relocate` renumbers the faces its walls hold (`massing::mirrored`). Nothing
else ties them to the mass, and IFC carries no mark: what comes back from a file is ordinary. `commands::category` reads `mass` and
`masses` as `mass` (it trims every trailing `s`, which would make `ma`). IFC writes a mass as an `IFCBUILDINGELEMENTPROXY` of object type
`Mass`, its footprint swept up; a lofted one is a closed `IFCTRIANGULATEDFACESET` with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set (`ifc::LOFT`) whose
`Loft` says as JSON how the footprint and the top outline pair up, since a face set doesn't. Import reads those before the proxies that
become components of families, and takes a lofted one only when that set's outlines are the body's bottom and its top; a mass whose
outline changes from base to top with no such set is left out and listed. The desktop's Massing tab has the Mass tool (`Tool::Mass`:
corners clicked, Enter or the first corner again finishes, `finish_mass`), Show Mass (the button is pressed while the view shows
masses) and, for each selected mass, the Model by Face buttons, which run the face commands, and Update to Face; a mass's Properties
hold its levels and offsets and `Top Outline`, its corners as `x, y` parted by `;`, blank for none.

Modify Sub Elements picks folding lines too, Revit's name for the creases no split line makes (`Model::shape_folds`,
  `view3d::shape_pick_plan`, `shape_pick_3d`), and Convert Lines makes the selected ones split lines, one way, as Revit's
  does (`SlabShapeEditor.CreateCreasesFromFoldingLines` in its API); tests `a_shapes_folding_lines_*`,
  `convert_lines_makes_a_selected_folding_line_a_split_line`.
- **Phase 4**, flat roofs, is built: a flat roof by footprint takes a shape through the same commands and tools
  (`Model::shapeable` sees its top as a floor's, `Model::roof_as_floor`), its underside following its top plumb
  (`roof_faces`, `roof_rise`), walls attached under it following its falls, its plan creases thin, its points snapped,
  kept by `edit_boundary` and carried by moves and mirrors; a pitched, extruded or joining roof refuses one, saying why
  (`Roof::unshapeable`). `ci/ifc-coverage.txt` has one for IfcOpenShell. Tests: the three `*roof*` tests in
  `shape_tests.rs`, and `a_flat_roof_by_footprint_is_shaped_as_a_floor_is_and_a_pitched_one_isnt` in the desktop's
  `tests/shape3d.rs`. A roof type's variable layer keeps a shaped roof's underside level at its base, as a floor's does
  (`Model::roof_under`, `roof_prisms`, `roof_solid`, `variable_under`): 3D layers, sections, attached walls, IFC (one
  closed Brep; `ci/ifc-coverage.txt` has both kinds) and the check (tests `a_roofs_variable_layer_*`,
  `a_section_shows_a_roofs_insulation_*`, `a_roof_point_that_would_leave_its_insulation_*`).
- **Phase 5**, the extras, is built:
  - **`falls`** (`crates/core/src/falls.rs`): a floor's or flat roof's shape from its drains and the least fall. Each
    drain takes the part of the outline nearer it than any other; where two parts meet a ridge runs at the top's height;
    from each drain a valley runs to each corner of its part; each drain goes down as far as the fall takes its farthest
    corner, to the tenth of a millimetre down. Every plane then falls at least as asked toward a drain, its lowest corner,
    and so does every valley. Round an opening, a valley runs from the drain round the opening's corners by the shortest
    way, each corner on the cone falling from the drain at the fall, so water reaching it runs on down. `ridges` drawn
    (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split the top into parts first, each needing a drain.
    The command checks every plane falls as asked to a drain or an opening's corner, and refuses, saying where, what
    doesn't. Refused too: a drain outside or in an opening, two within a millimetre, a corner a drain can reach only over
    the outline or a ridge (an L with one drain: add one on the other wing). Tests `falls_to_two_drains_*`,
    `falls_refuse_*`, `falls_run_round_an_opening_*`, `ridges_drawn_split_the_top_*`.
  - **IFC import of a slab whose top isn't one plane** (`import::shaped_top`): a level floor at its highest point, its
    upward faces' outline, each of their corners under that height (or inside) a point, and each edge two of them share at
    an angle a split line; as thick as it is under its highest corner. What doesn't fold into planes, or folds into others
    than its faces (a step), comes in as before. A roof's body read the same way comes in as a shaped flat roof, unless its
    footprint and pitch already make every corner of its top (a pitched roof stays pitched; an extruded one is read by its
    profile). A variable layer goes out with `Description` `'Variable'` and comes back marked; from a file that says
    nothing, a shaped slab whose underside is level gets its insulation nearest the top, else its substrate, marked
    variable. Tests `a_shaped_slab_exported_and_imported_*`, `a_shaped_floor_over_a_variable_layer_comes_back_*`,
    `a_shaped_flat_roof_comes_back_from_ifc_*`.
  - **Spot Slope** (`spot_slope`, `Spot::slope`, `Model::spot_slope`, `top_plane_at`): in a plan, an arrow downhill from
    the point clicked on a floor or a roof, with how steeply its top falls there, following it; Annotate > Dimension's
    Spot Slope places one. Tests `a_spot_slope_reads_*` and the desktop's
    `spot_slope_reads_the_fall_of_a_shaped_floor_where_its_clicked`.

Line numbers are as of `0733fd4`.

## What users expect

The workflow architects know from the established tools, in our own words:

- A floor (or a roof with no sloped edges) gets **points** on its top. Each point has a height relative to the top the
  element would have without them. The corners of the outline are points too, at 0 until raised or lowered.
- **Split lines** cross the top between two points. They are creases the surface must fold along, so the user decides
  where a ridge or a valley runs instead of leaving it to the triangulation.
- The surface between the points and lines is **flat triangles**. The tool picks the creases it needs and draws them
| `type` (floor, roof) | layers take `variable: true` | At most one per type; not on walls or ceilings. |
| `modify` (floor) | unchanged | Rejects `slope` or `arrow` on a shaped floor, with the reason (see Validation). |
| `falls` (phase 5) | `{id, drains: [[x, y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x, y], [x, y]], …]}` | Better than the established tools: sets point heights so water runs to the drains at no less than `fall` %, adding split lines along the valleys. Agents and architects describe a terrace this way, not point by point. |

Every reply lists the pieces' count and the lowest and highest point of the top. `inspect` on a floor already reports
`top: [lo, hi]` (`commands.rs:2122`); it must take the shape's points into account, not only the outline's.

## Validation (`Model::check`)

New rules, each with an error that says what to fix:

- A point outside the outline, or inside an opening: "point 100231 at (12500, 3400) is outside floor 100190: move it inside, or delete it".
- A split line that crosses another, crosses an opening, or leaves the outline (reuse `sketch::solve`'s problem kinds and wording).
- A split line end that is neither a point nor an outline corner.
- Two points within 1 mm of each other.
- A shape on a sloped floor (with `arrow`), or on a roof that isn't by footprint with `slope` 0. In version 1 the two are
  exclusive: shape a level element, and give its slope through the points.
- More than one variable layer in a type.
- **A variable layer thinner than nothing** anywhere: "at point 100231 the screed would be −12 mm: raise the point by 12
  mm or thicken the variable layer".
- With no variable layer, nothing bounds the depth: the slab just follows the top.

## What changes, consumer by consumer

| Consumer | Today | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `Model::floor_slabs` (`model.rs:3755`) | one plane over the outline less openings | built on `floor_faces`; each piece less the openings |
| `Model::roof_faces` (`model.rs:3575`) | a flat roof is one plane | a shaped flat roof returns its pieces; `roof_rise` is plumb for them |
| 3D solids (`view3d.rs:511`, `612`) | `Solid::Slab` per piece | the same for constant thickness; `Solid::Prism` (top facet, flat bottom) with a variable layer |
| 3D layers (`view3d::layered`, `view3d.rs:741`) | a slab's layers in proportion; the `Prism` branch is walls only | a slab `Prism` branch: layers above the variable one from the top, below it from the bottom |
| Section layers (`render.rs:1230`) | each cut quad split in proportion to the layers' thicknesses | the same rule as 3D: fixed layers measured from the top or the bottom edge, the variable one between |
| Plan (`render.rs:1585`) | outline, openings, surface pattern, slope arrow | the pattern over each piece; split lines solid and generated creases dashed, thin, when the element is selected or being edited; each point's height as a label while editing (built as the desktop's overlay, not in `render.rs`, so it never prints) |
| Attached walls (`walls.rs:454`) | one plane over the floor's convex pieces | each piece with its own plane, as the roof branch above it does |
| Shafts (`Model::less_shafts`, `model.rs:3773`) | per slab face | already per face: no change, but a test |
| Move, copy, rotate, mirror (`commands.rs:8236`) | outline, openings, arrow, pattern | the points' `at` and the lines' ends too; a mirror keeps the heights |

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

The script is 190:[`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md) 261:| Revit files (read only; the command line and the desktop) | A Revit `.rvt` or `.rfa` file of release 2015 to 2027 (checked on Autodesk's sample projects of 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, and the Snowdon Towers files) is read by a reader of its own, `crates/rvt`, ported in part from [rvt-rs](https://github.com/DrunkOnJava/rvt-rs) and fenced by [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md). `info` shows its release, build and document GUID, the last save (the saver's name when worksharing records it, and the path it was saved to; shown by `info`, never written into a project or an IFC file), the title, the levels with their names and elevations, and the number of elements in each `BuiltInCategory`, how many of them are placed instances. `run x.rvt`, `convert x.rvt out.ifc` and the MCP server's `open` import the file as a new project: its levels, straight and curved walls with their compound layers and materials (the exterior on the side the file's flip says), floors and ceilings from their sketches (holes and separate loops included), doors and windows in the walls that hold them, columns, rooms with their numbers and names, and roofs (by footprint, those that rise coming in level, and ones by extrusion whose profile is straight lines in a plane square to an axis and whose box the profile and the type's thickness reproduce to a millimetre), converted from feet to millimetres and checked by `Model::check`. Only what a record says is read, and the reply says what is not. Where the record's own box gives a stand-in (a curtain wall as the plane of its box, a sloped or stepped floor, ceiling or roof level at the bottom of its box, a sketch that closes nothing as the footprint of its box, a column as the rectangle of its box) the element comes in as that stand-in and a note in `skipped` says what was not read of it; that is an approximation, and it is not counted as read whole. Anything else the reader cannot decode (a roof by extrusion that is not a straight-line profile, a skylight, a room no walls enclose, stairs, groups, families) is left out and listed in the reply's `skipped` as `N kinds left out, why`. In the desktop, File > Open, the system's open event (Finder, Open With) and a file named on the command line take a `.rvt`: the window stays alive while a box says "Opening a Revit file", asks about unsaved changes first as for any file, and the project that comes in is new and unsaved (Save asks for a `.bimcraft` name; nothing is written back to the `.rvt`, and it is not in File > Open Recent). The status box says how many elements came in and how many were left out, and File > Revit import report lists what came in by category and the notes of what was left out, grouped by cause with their ids. A build without the reader has no `.rvt` option and says why. Joins are BIMCraft's own, and a door's swing is not read. Checked against rvt-rs's own IFC export of the same files, the imported walls, floors, ceilings, openings, columns and roofs agree to a fraction of a millimetre (walls differ where a join is a butt there and a mitre here). A file is read under limits (its size, its streams, what each inflates to) and a damaged or hostile one is an error that says what is wrong. Nothing is taken from inside the file (families, templates, icons) for BIMCraft's own content.
