/workspace/README.md:261:| Revit files (read only; the command line and the desktop) | A Revit `.rvt` or `.rfa` file of release 2015 to 2027 (checked on Autodesk's sample projects of 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, and the Snowdon Towers files) is read by a reader of its own, `crates/rvt`, ported in part from [rvt-rs](https://github.com/DrunkOnJava/rvt-rs) and fenced by [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md). `info` shows its release, build and document GUID, the last save (the saver's name when worksharing records it, and the path it was saved to; shown by `info`, never written into a project or an IFC file), the title, the levels with their names and elevations, and the number of elements in each `BuiltInCategory`, how many of them are placed instances. `run x.rvt`, `convert x.rvt out.ifc` and the MCP server's `open` import the file as a new project: its levels, straight and curved walls with their compound layers and materials (the exterior on the side the file's flip says), floors and ceilings from their sketches (holes and separate loops included), doors and windows in the walls that hold them, columns, rooms with their numbers and names, and roofs (by footprint, those that rise coming in level, and ones by extrusion whose profile is straight lines in a plane square to an axis and whose box the profile and the type's thickness reproduce to a millimetre), converted from feet to millimetres and checked by `Model::check`. Only what a record says is read, and the reply says what is not. Where the record's own box gives a stand-in (a curtain wall as the plane of its box, a sloped or stepped floor, ceiling or roof level at the bottom of its box, a sketch that closes nothing as the footprint of its box, a column as the rectangle of its box) the element comes in as that stand-in and a note in `skipped` says what was not read of it; that is an approximation, and it is not counted as read whole. Anything else the reader cannot decode (a roof by extrusion that is not a straight-line profile, a skylight, a room no walls enclose, stairs, groups, families) is left out and listed in the reply's `skipped` as `N kinds left out, why`. In the desktop, File > Open, the system's open event (Finder, Open With) and a file named on the command line take a `.rvt`: the window stays alive while a box says "Opening a Revit file", asks about unsaved changes first as for any file, and the project that comes in is new and unsaved (Save asks for a `.bimcraft` name; nothing is written back to the `.rvt`, and it is not in File > Open Recent). The status box says how many elements came in and how many were left out, and File > Revit import report lists what came in by category and the notes of what was left out, grouped by cause with their ids. A build without the reader has no `.rvt` option and says why. Joins are BIMCraft's own, and a door's swing is not read. Checked against rvt-rs's own IFC export of the same files, the imported walls, floors, ceilings, openings, columns and roofs agree to a fraction of a millimetre (walls differ where a join is a butt there and a mitre here). A file is read under limits (its size, its streams, what each inflates to) and a damaged or hostile one is an error that says what is wrong. Nothing is taken from inside the file (families, templates, icons) for BIMCraft's own content. Builds that include the reader are Apache-2.0 (see License); `--no-default-features` leaves it out |

"""Run each line of a file (or args) as its own `run --cmd` on a fresh project (with -f files

usage: each.py [-m] [-p prefixfile] [-f file] lines...  (or -i file of lines)
"""
import os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-aa380c34464cd9919/target/release/bimcraft-cli'
args = sys.argv[1:]
exe = ORIG
prefix = ''
files = []
lines = []
both = False
while args:
    a = args.pop(0)
    if a == '-m': exe = MINE
    elif a == '-b': both = True
    elif a == '-p': prefix = open(args.pop(0)).read()
    elif a == '-P': prefix += args.pop(0) + '\n'
    elif a == '-f': files.append(args.pop(0))
    elif a == '-i': lines += [l for l in open(args.pop(0)).read().split('\n') if l.strip()]
    else: lines.append(a)
def run(exe, line):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='e')
    for f in files:

    cmd = [exe, 'run'] + [os.path.basename(f) for f in files if f.endswith('.bimcraft')] + ['--script', 's.txt']
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=300)

You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md, design notes in /workspace/docs/, especially docs/areas/levels-walls-roofs.md, docs/areas/massing.md, docs/shape-editing.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Many agents work in parallel; you are a sub-agent of the ARCH agent (architecture: walls, floors, roofs, rooms, stairs, masses, sketches, shapes). You work in your own git worktree.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it ONLY by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, under /tmp/<your-name>/. Commit only Rust.
- Only edit the files you are told you own; the only other edits allowed are registering your module/commands in `src/arch/mod.rs` (a `pub mod` line, entries in `COMMANDS`, a dispatch arm, a check arm) or `src/geom/mod.rs` (a `pub mod` line). List any such edit in your final report.

## Getting started
1. Your worktree must start from the ARCH agent's commit 6a1b9e5 (branch `worktree-agent-aa380c34464cd9919`). Run `git log --oneline -1`; if HEAD isn't 6a1b9e5 (or a descendant of it), run `git reset --hard 6a1b9e5`.
2. Build with `cargo build --release` (about 15 s); the binary is `<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`.
3. Probe tools are in /tmp/arch-agent/tools (copy them to your own /tmp dir; each takes the env var `MINE=<your binary>`):
   - `o.py [-m] [-c cats] [-n] cmd1 cmd2 ...` runs commands as a script on a fresh project with the original (or yours with -m), prints replies and the saved elements.
   - `each.py [-b] [-P prefixcmd]... [-i file] lines...` runs each line as its own script (after the prefix commands) and prints the result of the last; `-b` runs both programs and marks SAME/DIFF.
   - `order.py [-p prefixcmd] cmd '{bad params}' '{good params}'` finds the order in which a command validates its parameters.
   - `craft.py [-b] base.bimcraft 'python on d / E' [cmd]` writes a modified copy of a project file, opens it and runs a command (the original checks the model when opening, so this shows the model's rule messages and their order).
   - `fl.py [-b] groups.txt` (env CATS, KEYS) runs groups of commands (blank-line separated) and prints chosen fields of chosen categories.
   - `MINE=<your binary> python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -- run --cmd '...' --cmd '...' --save x.bimcraft` runs both programs in fresh dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels exactly.
   - Useful: `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with each command's `params` text.

## The codebase (read what you need; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), `jobj!{}`, `to_compact`, `kind_name()` (serde's "invalid type" wording), float formatting identical to serde_json.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order: `guid`, `category`, then its struct's fields) + `library` (`{kind, name, guid}`: types are kind `type:wall` etc., families `family`, family types `family-type` named "Family: Type"); `alloc_id()`, `find_guid`, `guid_of`, `lib_guid(kind, name)`, `lib_name(guid)`. Elements reference levels, hosts, types… by GUID in the file.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` runs a command, then `crate::arch::check_edits(before, after, cid)` (outline simplicity of what changed) and `crate::check::check` (every module's `check(pr)`; ARCH's is `crate::arch::check`, which runs each element's rules in id order, then cross-element rules), rolls back on any error, and records an undo step labelled by the catalog label.
- `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers with the original's texts (`req_num`, `opt_num` "must be a number in mm", `opt_text`, `opt_bool`, `req_point`, `opt_point`, `point_of`, `id_of`; |mm| <= 1e9). `src/model.rs`: `levels`, `elev`, `level_param`/`resolve_level` (with the original's errors), `level_above`, `find`, `normalize_guid`.
- ARCH so far (`src/arch/`): `util.rs` (helpers: `d(x)` = Rust Display of f64 as the messages print numbers, `dp(p)`, `num/numd/text/flag/pt/pts/rings` accessors, `pv/ring_v/rings_v`, `cat`, `by_ref`/`ref_word`/`ref_value`, `level_of`, `elev`, `level_guid`, `level_name`, `computation_height`, `type_names`, `type_def`, `type_guid`, `type_name`, `default_type`, `type_ref`, `check_type`, `thickness`, `layers`, `opt_ref`, `m2` (area mm² → m² 2 decimals), `put`), `walls.rs` (`Wall` struct: location line, centre line, `arc()`, `length()`, `base()`, `top()`, `spans(z)`; `cmd_wall`, `make_wall`, `cmd_flip`, `check_wall`, `joined_centres`), `openings.rs` (doors/windows, marks `next_series`), `slabs.rs` (floor/ceiling/shaft commands and checks, `clean`, `de_rings`/`de_points` serde-like readers, `opt_boundary`, `check_rings`), `roofs.rs` (roof command and checks, `wall_footprint`, `round3`), `rooms.rs` (room, room_separator, `space_at` room regions at centre lines and faces), `outline.rs` (`level_outline`: a level's wall outline and courtyards), `edits.rs` (`check_edits`), `mod.rs` (dispatch + `check`).
- `src/geom/`: `mod.rs` (P2 = [f64; 2] and vector ops, `area`, `inside`, `seg_dist`, `Arc` (centre, radius, a0, sweep) and `straight`), `graph.rs` (planar graph of segments: `Graph::build`, `faces()` traced as the original does; `arc_points`), `offset.rs` (`offset_ring` per-edge offsets), `sketch.rs` (a first sketch problem engine: `Problem`, `describe`, `ring_problems`, `parse`, `solve_one`, `to_value`), `tri.rs` (empty).
- Other areas are done by other agents (don't implement them): `modify`, `move`, `copy`, `delete` etc. (EDIT), `inspect`, `elements`, `schedule` (READERS), views/graphics (VIEWS), types/families/structure (STRUCTURE), IFC. Our build does not have them yet, so test your commands through scripts that use only ARCH commands plus `level`, `grid`, `undo`, `redo`, `save`, `open`.
- New elements get their phase/option with `crate::styles::phasing::stamp_new(&s.project, s.now_phase.as_deref(), s.now_option.as_deref(), &mut e)` before insertion (see `walls::make_wall`).

## How to work
Probe the original widely: normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases, every error and the order of checks (`order.py`), and what the saved file holds (field order, defaults omitted or written, number formatting). Write the code, then compare with `each.py -b` / `fl.py -b` / `cmp.py` until SAME. Error texts must match character for character (numbers in messages are usually Rust's `{}` Display of f64; points `[x, y]`). Keep a list of what still differs.

## Finish
Commit your work on your worktree branch (`git add -A && git commit -m "..."`), and make your final message a concise report: the branch name and commit, per command what matches and what doesn't, any edits outside your files, and any function other code must call (or that you need from others).

import math
cr = lambda p, q: p[0]*q[1] - p[1]*q[0]
sub = lambda p, q: (p[0]-q[0], p[1]-q[1])
add = lambda p, q: (p[0]+q[0], p[1]+q[1])
sc = lambda p, k: (p[0]*k, p[1]*k)
dot = lambda p, q: p[0]*q[0] + p[1]*q[1]
def unit(v):
    l = math.hypot(v[0], v[1]); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
def unit_s(v):
    l = math.sqrt(v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1]); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
E0 = ((0.0, 0.0), (10000.0, 0.0))
cases = [((703.0, 6000.0), 7283.499999999998), ((0.0, 3000.0), 7283.500000000002), ((1000.0, 6000.0), 7283.500000000001),
         ((2000.0, 6000.0), 7283.500000000001), ((3000.0, 6000.0), 7283.500000000001), ((4000.0, 6000.0), 7283.500000000001),
         ((10000.0, 3000.0), 7283.500000000001)]
end = (7283.5, 0.0)
def q_forms(cs, ce, os, oe):
    out = {}
    d = sub(ce, cs); e = sub(oe, os)
    for un_name, un in (('h', unit), ('s', unit_s)):
        u = un(d); ue = un(e)
        # distance along u to the host line
        s = cr(sub(os, cs), e) / cr(u, e)
        out['u_s_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, s))
        s2 = cr(sub(os, cs), ue) / cr(u, ue)
        out['u_ue_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, s2))
        n = (-ue[1], ue[0])
        s3 = dot(sub(os, cs), n) / dot(u, n)
        out['u_n_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, s3))
        # length based: start + u * |d| (no join, just recompute end)
        out['u_len_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, math.hypot(d[0], d[1])))
        out['u_len2_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, math.sqrt(d[0]*d[0] + d[1]*d[1])))
    t = cr(sub(os, cs), e) / cr(d, e)
    out['plain'] = add(cs, sc(d, t))
    return out
def finals(q, cs):
    out = {}
    a0, a1 = E0
    dd = sub(a1, a0); l2 = dot(dd, dd)
    t = dot(sub(q, a0), dd) / l2
    out['proj'] = add(a0, sc(dd, t))[0]
    # crossing of D (cs->q) with E0 along E0
    e = sub(q, cs); den = cr(dd, e)
    tt = cr(sub(cs, a0), e) / den
    out['cross'] = add(a0, sc(dd, tt))[0]
    out['raw'] = q[0]
    return out
table = {}
for cs, want in cases:
    qs = q_forms(cs, end, E0[0], E0[1])
    for qn, q in qs.items():
        for fn, v in finals(q, cs).items():
            table.setdefault((qn, fn), []).append(v == want)
for k, v in sorted(table.items(), key=lambda kv: -sum(kv[1])):
    print('%-14s %-6s %d/%d %s' % (k[0], k[1], sum(v), len(v), ''.join('1' if x else '.' for x in v)))

def unit(v):
    l = math.hypot(v[0], v[1]); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
def unit_s(v):
    l = math.sqrt(v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1]); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
E0 = ((0.0, 0.0), (10000.0, 0.0))

end = (7283.5, 0.0)
def q_forms(cs, ce, os, oe):
    out = {}
    d = sub(ce, cs); e = sub(oe, os)
    for un_name, un in (('h', unit), ('s', unit_s)):
        u = un(d); ue = un(e)
        # distance along u to the host line
        s = cr(sub(os, cs), e) / cr(u, e)
        out['u_s_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, s))
        s2 = cr(sub(os, cs), ue) / cr(u, ue)
        out['u_ue_' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, s2))

door : {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window : {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

floor : {boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its 

ceiling : {point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it

sketch : {lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about (numbered from 0): ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line too: a polyline round a bow tie crosses itself), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight

shaft : {boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`

edit_boundary : {id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The outline must be simple, as `floor` says; a line that crosses itself is found as two that cross are

edit_shape : {id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height th

add_point : {id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height

add_split_line : {id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now

reset_shape : {id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again

falls : {id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew 

mass : {boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofte

mass_floors : {mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volu

wall_by_face : {mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

floor_by_face : {mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on

roof_by_face : {mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on

update_by_face : {mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`

show_mass : {view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's

room : {point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless 

room_separator : {points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

stair : {start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or righ

ramp : {start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level

railing : {host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are

roof : {level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over `boundary` or else the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces, round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room i

dormer : {host, at: [x, y], width?, height?, slope?, window?, type?} a dormer on roof `host`, its front wall across the slope through `at`: walls of `type` `width` mm (1600) apart, standing on the roof and `height` mm (1200) tall at the front, under a gable roof of its own sloping `slope` degrees (30) that runs back into the host; the host open under it, and with `window` (a window type) a window in its front. Replies with its roof, walls and window

flip : {ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

def meet(a0, a1, b0, b1):
    d = sub(a1, a0); e = sub(b1, b0); den = cr(d, e)
    t = cr(sub(b0, a0), e) / den
    return add(a0, sc(d, t))
def proj(a0, a1, p):
    d = sub(a1, a0); t = dot(sub(p, a0), d) / dot(d, d)
    return add(a0, sc(d, t))

import json, sys, subprocess, tempfile, os, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-aa380c34464cd9919/target/release/bimcraft-cli'
args = sys.argv[1:]
both = False
if args and args[0] == '-b':
    both = True
    args = args[1:]
base, code = args[0], args[1]
cmd = args[2] if len(args) > 2 else 'level {"elevation": 90000}'
d = json.load(open(base))
E = {int(k): v for k, v in d['elements'].items()}
def guid(i):
    return E[i]['guid']
exec(code)
d['elements'] = {str(k): v for k, v in sorted(E.items())}
def run(exe):
    t = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    json.dump(d, open(os.path.join(t, 'c.bimcraft'), 'w'), indent=2)
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'run', 'c.bimcraft', '--cmd', cmd], cwd=t, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(t)
    return (p.stdout.decode() + p.stderr.decode()).strip()
o = run(ORIG)
print('O:', o)
if both:
    m = run(MINE)
    print('M:', m)

content.text:
I've finished the ARCH area. It's committed on branch `worktree-agent-aa380c34464cd9919`, latest commit `208af63`, with a clean tree. Almost everything matches the original exactly; the differences left are mostly last-digit rounding (about 1e-13) on diagonal walls and arcs.

**Checks run:** a regression suite of 110 script files run on both programs, comparing replies, errors and saved files with GUIDs normalised: 1210 groups the same, 87 different. Of the 87, 27 are `modify` lines (an edit command my build doesn't have), 3 use `column`, which my build lacks, and the rest are the rounding cases listed below. The fuzzers on new seeds had no differences (3 × 80 parameter runs, 3 × 40 random command sequences). The unit tests pass.

**Fixed this session:**
- **Floors from walls:** the outline now starts at the same corner as the original's, including when a dangling wall is drawn before the loop. This also fixed some overlapping-loop and diagonal cases.
- **T-junctions:** a later wall's or separator's end on an earlier line now lands where the original puts it, including the case within 1 mm of a corner, where the original treats a line's start and end differently.
- **Rooms:**
  - Rooms now read walls first, then room separators, then columns; this decides where frozen rooms' saved outlines start.
  - Adding a room no longer recomputes every earlier room; 30 rooms over 122 walls went from 10.3 s to 1.1 s of CPU (the original takes 5.8 s).
- **Inputs given as arrays:** `roof extrusion`, stair/ramp `landings` and `edit_shape` points and lines now accept the field-list form, with the original's error texts. Shape points and lines also validate `id`/`guid` as the original does.
- **Shape point ids after `open`:** new point and line ids now go below the ones already in the file, as the original's do.

**Per command:**
- **Same in every test:** `door`, `window`, `shaft`, `dormer`, `room_separator`, `stair`, `ramp`, `railing`, `mass`, `mass_floors`, `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face`, `roof_by_face`, `update_by_face`, `show_mass`, `add_point`, `add_split_line`, `reset_shape`, `flip`, and `roof` (all forms).
- **`wall`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `room`, `sketch`, `edit_boundary`, `edit_shape`:** match, except where diagonal walls join or arcs are traced. There my wall-join arithmetic differs from the original's; for example, a closed triangle's corner comes out as exactly 0 in mine and 6.5e-14 in the original. Arc points differ in the last digits. Also:
  - Frozen rooms' saved outline at the wall faces differs in the last digits on diagonals.
  - A room separator ending inside a wall near a corner gives a different face outline.
  - With an "exterior-finish" loop plus an overlapping interior wall, one corner is off in the last digit.
  - I spent a long time trying to reproduce the original's join arithmetic and couldn't find the exact formula.
- **`falls`:** fo1 20/20, fr2 12/14. Still different: a drain exactly on a diagonal ridge, and a single ridge from the outline to an opening where the original says the top "can't fall".

**Edits outside `src/arch` and `src/geom` (6 lines, unchanged since before):**
- `src/main.rs`: `pub mod geom;`
- `src/session.rs`: calls `crate::arch::check_edits(before, after, cid)` before `crate::check::check`.
- `src/styles/parameters.rs`: adds `"Mass Face"` to `RESERVED`.

**What other areas must provide or call:**
- **Readers:** the loader should run `crate::check::check` on open, with errors as `open: {path}: {msg}`. They can use:
  - `rooms::room_area`, `room_space`, `space_at`, `region_at_faces`, `column_outline`
  - `slabs::net_area`, `openings::opening_size`, `stairs::layout`, `railing_path`, `risers`, `stair_length`, `ramp_length`
  - `roofs::roof_faces`, `ridge`, `outline`, `plan_area`, `eave_height`, `mass::Mass`, `slices`
- **Edit:** `move`, `rotate` and `mirror` must also transform frozen rooms' saved outlines and shape points. My outline check lets these commands through unchecked.
- **IFC and views:**
  - `walls::footprint`, `walls::joined_centres`, `walls::Wall`
  - `hosts::pieces`, `z_at`, `wall_heights`, `height_along`
  - `shape::lift` with the new `geom::tri::plane_groups` (which triangles merge into each face of a shaped top), plus `geom::skeleton`, `geom::tri` and `geom::graph`. The shaped-floor asset's top face count (6) matches what `edit_shape` reports.
  - One difference: the IFC wall profile includes the centre-line corner points, but `walls::footprint` gives a plain 4-corner ring.
- **Shared code:**
  - `project.rs` `lowest_lib_id` doesn't look at ids stored inside elements. I work around it for shape ids, but other areas allocating ids after `open` could collide.
  - `cloud::file::ref_of` accepts `"+5"` as an id; the original rejects it.
- **Structure:** rooms read `column` and `structuralcolumn` elements; my build has no `column` command.

Scratch scripts and test inputs are in `/tmp/arch-agent/` (`reg2.py` runs the regression).
